newsitem.title: USA: Albright takes firm positions on China, Cuba.
newsitem.headline: Albright takes firm positions on China, Cuba.

text.p: Madeleine Albright, declaring her intent to speak "plainly," faced journalists for the first time as secretary of state on Friday and quickly took firm positions on China, Cuba and Sudan.

Looking confident and ebullient in her new role as America's first female secretary of state, Albright fielded questions from a State Department briefing room packed full of reporters and more than two dozen TV and still cameras.

But she broke no new ground in U.S. policy and sidestepped touchy questions on the extent of Saudi Arabia's cooperation in bringing to justice those who bombed a U.S. military housing complex in the kingdom last June.
Albright, 59, former U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, was sworn in to office on Thursday as Warren Christopher's successor and quickly got down to work.

Her first substantive meeting, lasting 90 minutes, focused on China, officials said. She was briefed for several hours on Friday on a wide array of issues before the news conference, which was part of a campaign to introduce her to America and the world.
She told reporters she would make an around the world trip to Europe and Asia next month, but details were not complete.
She vowed to "tell it like it is" to China on human rights issues and the future of Hong Kong, but reaffirmed the U.S. view that Sino-American ties could not be held hostage to any one issue.

"I will tell it like it is on the human rights issues and on Hong Kong to the Chinese when I meet with them," she said, adding that the broad U.S.-China agenda "cannot be held hostage to any one issue."

She noted Beijing's positive dealings with Washington on North Korea and Cambodia, but added: "There are some on which we differ -- and human rights is one of them ... So we have made it clear that ... what happens with Hong Kong is very important to the overall relationship."
Albright's first telephone call from a foreign leader was from British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind and they agreed to work together on Hong Kong, she said.
Washington has voiced concern over China's handling of the leadup to Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule on June 30.
Albright promised Washington would maintain its tough isolationist policy on Cuba and said it was a mistake to have a "romantic view" of communist leader Fidel Castro.
"Cuba is an embarrassment to the Western hemisphere and I think we need to keep making clear that there needs to be a change there," she said.

The new secretary said Washington would seek new U.N. sanctions on Sudan because of its alleged support for terrorism. "We will continue to insist that Sudan desist from supporting terrorist activities and will be following up in New York to try to get additional sanctions," she said.

Officials said she referred to a U.S. effort to persuade the U.N. to implement a flight ban approved last year on Sudan Airways. The ban was part of a package of mandatory penalties against Sudan for not extraditing three men wanted for trying to kill Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in 1995.
Sudan is one of seven countries on a State Department list of states alleged to support terrorism.

Albright stressed the U.S. desire for NATO enlargement, but also emphasised the need to resolve differences with Russia over this fractious issue. She also reiterated support for the U.S. policy of dual containment toward Iraq and Iran.

Her most important task will be "sustaining momentum toward the creation of a Europe that is united, stable and democratic, and in an Asian-Pacific community that cooperates increasingly based on shared economic interests and a common commitment to peace," she said.

She laughingly referred to the fact she had "been under wraps for a while," declining to speak to reporters until she was confirmed by the Senate and sworn in. But now, she said, she would be "open ... speak plainly and leave the rhetoric aside." She has been besieged with requests for interviews and will appear on CNN on Friday, NBC on Sunday and ABC on Monday.
Albright said top-level State Department appointments would be announced soon by the White House.
